title: API Security Best Practices: A Practical Threat-Modeling Checklist
description: How to protect APIs with clear authorization rules, safe data handling, abuse controls, testing, and incident response.
author: PilotStack Team

sections.title: Model assets, actors, and trust boundaries
sections.body: List the sensitive data, operations, and business actions exposed by the API. Identify users, service accounts, administrators, third-party clients, and anonymous callers. Draw the boundaries between the public internet, application services, databases, and external providers. For each endpoint, document who may call it, which objects they may access, and which state changes they may perform. This prevents security reviews from stopping at a generic statement that the API uses authentication.

sections.title: Enforce object- and action-level authorization
sections.body: Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines what that identity can do. Check permissions for each requested object and action on the server, including list, export, update, and delete operations. Do not rely on hidden UI controls or client-supplied role values. Test cross-tenant access with accounts from different tenants and verify that identifiers cannot be used to retrieve another customer's records. Review permission changes and administrative endpoints separately.

sections.title: Validate inputs and protect outputs
sections.body: Define allowed formats, lengths, ranges, and enumerated values for every input. Use parameterized database operations, safe serialization, and explicit content-type handling. Return only fields the caller needs, and avoid exposing stack traces, internal identifiers, or secrets in error messages. Set request-size limits and timeouts. Treat uploaded files, callback URLs, webhooks, and user-provided URLs as untrusted inputs that may require additional validation and network restrictions.

sections.title: Manage credentials and sessions safely
sections.body: Use established identity libraries and modern token validation rather than hand-written cryptography. Verify issuer, audience, expiration, and signature; rotate credentials and revoke access when staff or integrations change. Store secrets in an appropriate secret manager and never commit them to source control or include them in logs. Scope API keys narrowly, separate production from test credentials, and monitor unusual use. Document the recovery process for a leaked credential.

sections.title: Control abuse and resource exhaustion
sections.body: Apply rate limits and quotas according to identity, endpoint sensitivity, and resource cost. Protect expensive search, export, and report endpoints separately from lightweight reads. Consider pagination caps, concurrency limits, request deadlines, and bounded retries. Return clear rate-limit responses and monitor patterns that indicate credential stuffing, scraping, or automated abuse. Limits should protect service stability without blocking legitimate clients unexpectedly.

sections.title: Test security continuously
sections.body: Include authorization tests, input validation, dependency checks, secret scanning, and negative tests in CI. Use a staging environment to test realistic attack paths without exposing production data. Review API schema changes for newly exposed fields or operations. Keep a process for reporting vulnerabilities and prioritizing fixes by impact. Passing an automated scanner is useful evidence, but it does not prove that business-specific authorization logic is correct.

sections.title: Prepare for incidents and reassessment
sections.body: Log security-relevant events without recording sensitive payloads or credentials. Define who investigates suspected abuse, how to revoke keys, how to contain an affected endpoint, and how customers will be notified if required. Preserve enough evidence to reconstruct the event. Reassess the threat model when new integrations, data types, roles, or endpoints are added. Security is an ongoing release requirement, not a one-time configuration.
